# Crowbook

Crowbook lets you write a book in Markdown and generate HTML, PDF and EPUB output without worrying about formatting or typography.

It focuses on novels and fiction and provides sensible defaults to produce readable books with correct typography.

## Example

To see Crowbook's output examples, see the project's published book pages (HTML, PDF, EPUB) on the project's website or releases.

## Installing

Download a precompiled binary for your platform from the project's releases page and place the executable somewhere on your PATH.

## Usage

The simplest invocation is:

    $ crowbook <BOOK>

where <BOOK> is a book configuration file. Crowbook will parse this file and generate HTML, EPUB, and/or PDF output according to the settings.

For short texts contained in a single Markdown file, Crowbook can accept a single Markdown file with embedded metadata and produce output directly.

## Output formats

Crowbook supports HTML, PDF and EPUB as output formats.

Note: Generating PDF output typically requires a working LaTeX installation (for example, xelatex) on your system.

## Input format

Crowbook accepts CommonMark-like Markdown input. You can also include a small metadata block (YAML) at the top of a single Markdown file to set title/author and other options when running in single-file mode.

## Customization

Templates allow you to customize the visual appearance of the generated books. See the project's documentation for template usage and examples.

## Bugs and support

Report issues on the project's issue tracker (link available on the project's website or GitHub repository page).

- **French typography corner cases:**

- **PDF:** with no `xelatex` installed, I reproduce the original's error message. I haven't tested real PDF generation.

Templates, the original's help text and its embedded menu/book SVG icons are stored as files under `templates/`.

- **Typography:** curly quotes; French non-breaking spaces before `: ; ! ?`, around `« »`, after dialogue dashes and between numbers and units.

- **French spacing:** spaced hyphens (as opposed to `—` or `–`) don't fully match the original's rules.

That includes the README and LGPL licence rendered as a book, and EPUB contents once the random UUID and timestamp are masked out. On random Markdown, about 96% of English cases match exactly, and about 90% of French cases when hyphens are left out. My binary never crashed on any of the random inputs.

**Where it can still differ:**
- **Code highlighting:** I approximated the original's colours for Rust, Python, JavaScript, JSON, YAML, shell, C/Java/Go, HTML and SQL. HTML output matches my samples for every language except CSS (left uncoloured), plus a small Go difference. LaTeX region boundaries can still differ, and every other language falls back to plain text, which will differ wherever the original highlights.
- **French spacing:** spaced hyphens (as opposed to `—` or `–`) don't fully match the original's rules.
- **Autolinks:** emails and URLs inside unclosed `[` brackets sometimes link differently.
- **Unmatchable by design:** EPUB files can't be byte-identical, because of the UUID, timestamp and zip compression. Verbose (`-v`) output includes timestamps and thread IDs. Warning order when several formats render at once is nondeterministic in the original itself; I copied its most common order.

`./compile.sh` replaces `./executable`, so running it in place overwrites the original binary. I could only run the original, not copy it, so I built and tested in a separate clone.
